intended_object: The value of the static Schrödinger problem, inf { H(π | R) : π a coupling of μ and ν }, with H the relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence) against a reference measure R on X × Y. This comes from the docstring, the module documentation and the cited references (Léonard; Nutz).
explanation:
The body takes the infimum of Mathlib's `klDiv π R` over all measures π with `IsCoupling π μ ν`. `IsCoupling` is defined in the library as `π.fst = μ ∧ π.snd = ν`. The infimum is iterated over plans and over proofs of `IsCoupling`, so an empty feasible set gives `⊤ = ∞`, which is what the docstring says. This is exactly the static Schrödinger value inf_{π ∈ Π(μ,ν)} H(π|R).

The setting is fully general: arbitrary measurable spaces, arbitrary measures μ, ν and R, and Mathlib's general `klDiv`. Nothing is specialised.

When R is a probability measure, as in Nutz's notes and most of the literature, `klDiv` is the usual relative entropy, so the value is the textbook one. When R is a finite measure, Mathlib's `klDiv` adds the mass term R(X×Y) − π(X×Y). This is the standard I-divergence of finite measures. On couplings that term is the constant R(X×Y) − μ(X), so the value is only shifted and the minimizers are the same.

The only real departure is a non-finite reference measure, as in Léonard's setting where R can be unbounded. There Mathlib's `klDiv` differs from ∫ log(dπ/dR) dπ, because it truncates at 0 and drops the infinite mass. But the docstring explicitly defines the value through `klDiv`, and the library's results assume a finite R. So this is a convention, not an error.

Mathlib has no Schrödinger problem or entropic optimal transport value, so there is no counterpart to cite.
